WORLD SIGHT DAY · 10.8

Exploring the Shape of Life:
Geerat Vermeij

 

10.8 World Sight Day Recognition — The palm knows what the eye misses.

“The palm knows what the eye misses.”

 

Geerat Vermeij is a professor at UC Davis who specializes in evolutionary biology and geology. He uses his sense of touch to navigate the wonders of life — the shape of shells. His tactile experiences uncover insights about humanity, ecology, biology, and economics. He described the remnants of all living things as “works of art”, regardless of the fact that he lost his sight at the age of three.

Image description: Geerat Vermeij holds a shell specimen in front of archival drawers, reflecting his long study of natural form.

profile

From academic training to shell form

Professor Vermeij graduated from Princeton University in 1968, and earned his PhD at Yale University in 1971. As a biologist and paleontologist, he has published more than 250 scientific papers. In 1992, he was honored with the MacArthur Fellowship and elected for the Daniel Giraud Elliot Medal by the National Academy of Sciences in 2000.

 

··· ︵ ···

method

Tactile morphology

Professor Vermeij is known for practicing his unique “tactile morphology” methodology, using his fingertips to “feel” the world and to decode the microscopic contours, thickness variations, and surface ridges of shells to understand how they adapted to their environment.

Image description: Vermeij explores a shell specimen by touch, reading its spines, contours, and surface ridges.

Ornamental plate: shell photographs used as visual texture, echoing spirals, growth lines, and tactile research.

 

··· ︵ ···

evolution

Evolutionary arms races in shells

One of the most interesting focuses of his research is uncovering the “arms race” present among shell species: like the weaponry competition in human conflicts, the structure of shells also evolved in response to pressures from enemies, competitors, and predators. For instance, healed-over breakages on shells disclose the defense attempts of the shells and the attacks of predators. This discovery is synthesized as the Hypothesis of Escalation, mirroring how human societies utilize tools and defense strategies in response to rival groups.

Healed-over breakages on shells disclose both defense and attack.

 

Image description: A self-repaired conch, its healed break leaving a visible seam and altered edge along the shell.

fieldwork

Into the field

Contrary to the misconception that visually disabled scientists can only work in laboratories or desk roles, Professor Vermeij insisted on an active work style, traveling around the world — from the tropics of Costa Rica and Hawaii to other international coasts — to physically source and collect specimens in person.

Image description: During fieldwork, Vermeij examines shell fossils embedded in a coastal rock surface.
